sec:
Vote by mail or absentee

Can’t get to your polling place on Election Day? Here is how to vote by mail in Florida, from the state’s own election office and its laws. Checked October 21, 2026.

Ask for your ballot by

Thursday, October 22Passed

To have a ballot mailed to you: by 5 p.m. on Thursday, October 22, 2026 (the 12th day before the election). After that you can still pick one up in person, with the emergency statement described above. (official page)

Send it back by

Tuesday, November 3Passed

Your voted ballot must be RECEIVED by your county Supervisor of Elections by 7:00 p.m. local time on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3, 2026, no matter when it was postmarked. Late ballots are not counted (overseas voters have an exception, below). The U.S. Postal Service suggests mailing at least a week before. (official page)

The last day to ask for a ballot by mail has passed. You can still vote in person, early or on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3.You can still vote in person on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3. Early voting in person runs through Saturday, October 31, 2026. When and where to vote early.

Ask for a ballot online, on Florida’s own site

At school away from home, in Florida or in another state? What Florida says about students is under Show more.

Who can vote by mail

No reason is asked for. The state's page lists who may ask the county Supervisor of Elections for a vote-by-mail ballot: the voter, a close family member, a legal guardian, or a person named by a voter with a disability. (official page)

How to ask for a ballot

  • Online. Each county's Supervisor of Elections takes requests online; the state lists every county's link. Open it (official page)
  • By phone. Call your county Supervisor of Elections. Open it (official page)
  • Mail, fax or email. Sign the statewide request form (DS-DE 160) and send it to your county Supervisor of Elections by mail, fax, or as a scanned email attachment. If you want the ballot sent to an address different from the one on your record (for example a school address), the request must be in writing and signed. Open it (official page)
  • In person. Ask at your county Supervisor of Elections' office. You may pick up your own ballot there, including on Election Day. From the start of early voting on, picking up a ballot (yourself or through someone you name) also takes a signed statement that an emergency keeps you from voting at an early voting site or your polling place. (official page)

How to send it back

  • By mail. By the U.S. Postal Service or a private delivery company, as long as it arrives by 7:00 p.m. on Election Day. (official page)
  • Drop box. Secure drop boxes ("secure ballot intake stations") at the Supervisor of Elections' main and branch offices until 7:00 p.m. on Election Day, and at early voting sites. They are open only during set hours and are watched by staff; your county's website lists places and times. (official page)
  • In person. Hand it in at your county Supervisor of Elections' office by 7:00 p.m. on Election Day. A mail ballot cannot be returned online, by email or by fax (overseas voters may fax). (official page)

What the envelope needs

To ask for a ballot you give your Florida driver license number, Florida ID card number, or the last four digits of your Social Security number. Sign the voter's certificate on the return envelope. If your signature is missing or does not match, the county must tell you; fix it with the Vote-by-Mail Ballot Cure form and a copy of an ID by 5 p.m. on Thursday, November 5, 2026 (the 2nd day after the election). (official page)

Track your ballot

Track your ballot on Florida’s own site (official page)

Vote early in person instead

Saturday, October 24, 2026 to Saturday, October 31, 2026.

Every county offers early voting from Saturday, October 24 through Saturday, October 31, 2026. Some counties add optional days (as early as the 15th day and as late as the 2nd day before the election); ask your Supervisor of Elections. (official page)

Students

At school in Florida, away from home

The state's pages do not speak to students separately. Its general rules: you ask for your mail ballot from the Supervisor of Elections in the county where you are registered, and you may have it sent to an address other than the one on your record (such as a school address) if your request is in writing and signed. (official page)

At school in another state, with Florida as home

The state's pages do not speak to students separately. Its general rules: you ask the Supervisor of Elections in your county of registration; a mail ballot can be sent to an address other than the one on your record if your request is written and signed; and a ballot mailed from inside the U.S. must arrive by 7:00 p.m. on Election Day, whatever its postmark. (official page)

Military and overseas

Register and request with the federal FPCA form, online, or by the county's usual ways. Your blank ballot can come by mail, email or fax. Return it by mail, in person, or (overseas only) by fax to the number your Supervisor of Elections gives. Ballots must arrive by 7:00 p.m. on Election Day, except that an overseas voter's MAILED ballot counts in a general election if postmarked or dated by Election Day and received within 10 days after (by Friday, November 13, 2026). The Federal Write-in Absentee Ballot is a backup if yours has not come. (official page)

Florida in the Federal Voting Assistance Program’s guide

Good to know

  • The request deadline is Thursday, October 22, 2026, at 5 p.m., one day after this record was checked.
  • Florida counts a domestic mail ballot only if it ARRIVES by 7:00 p.m. on Election Day; a postmark does not help.
  • The 10-day window for overseas ballots is counted here as November 13, 2026 (ten days after November 3); the state gives only the rule.

Checked October 21, 2026. Rules and dates can change: Florida’s election office, and your county or local election office, have the final word.

polls:
Polls are open 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. local time. (the law)

  • rest of the state: 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. EST
  • The western Panhandle, west of the Apalachicola River: 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. CST

Anyone in line when the polls close may still vote.
